FRONT_BOARD:
## Before You Board

You are about to spend one night in an airport that does not want you to leave.

You don't read this book from front to back. Most sections end with a choice, and each choice sends you to a numbered section. Turn there, read on, choose again.

Some choices will save you. Some will cost you things you can't get back. A few will kill you, and when they do, the book will tell you where to start again.

Before you go any further, decide one thing.

Your father called you **Kite**, because you always flew off. But who were you to him?

*His son.* Write **SON** on your Adventure Sheet.

*His daughter.* Write **DAUGHTER** on your Adventure Sheet.

*Neither, or both, or something he never quite found the word for. Just his kid.* Write **KID** on your Adventure Sheet.

Now choose how you want to travel.

**Story Mode.** Don't roll for your scores. Write down **Nerve 9**, **Vigour 20** and **Fortune 9**, which makes your Fear limit 12.

When you are asked to test your Nerve or your Fortune, when something is chasing you, or when you have to fight, choose the outcome you'd like and turn there. (Don't subtract from your Fortune when you choose a Fortune result.) You can still be Claimed, and you can still be frightened past your limit. The airport plays fair, but it plays.

**Survival Mode.** Roll for your Nerve, Vigour and Fortune on the next page, and play every test, every chase and every fight by the dice. Nothing is guaranteed.

Your flight is LV 137. It is 11:52pm.

Turn to section 1.
FRONT_RULES:
## How the Airport Works

**Nerve.** Your steadiness. In Survival Mode, roll one die and add 6. In Story Mode, it is 9. To test your Nerve, roll two dice: if the total is equal to or under your Nerve, you succeed.

**Vigour.** Your body. In Survival Mode, roll two dice and add 12. In Story Mode, it is 20. It can't rise above its starting score. When it reaches 0, you sit down on the carpet and can't get up (see **Checkpoints**).

**Fortune.** In Survival Mode, roll one die and add 6. In Story Mode, it is 9. To test your Fortune, roll two dice: equal to or under it, you are Lucky. Either way, subtract 1 from your Fortune afterwards. If your Fortune is 0 or less, you are always Unlucky.

**Fear** starts at 0, and can never fall below 0. Your limit is your Nerve plus 3, which is 12 in Story Mode. If your Fear reaches its limit, turn straight to {E_FINALCALL}.

**Claim** starts at 0. The airport is writing your name down, one letter at a time. It adds a letter every time you give your name away, every time it learns your face, and every time you die. The book will say: "Add 1 to your Claim." If your Claim reaches 4, the seat meant for you will not take you: the true ending is closed to you. If it reaches 5, turn straight to {E_FINALCALL}.

**Hours.** Your Adventure Sheet has six boxes for the hours from midnight to 06:00. Tick one hour each time you come back to the Atrium from a zone: the Concourse, the Duty-Free or the Hotel. Your first arrival in the Atrium, from Gate 14, doesn't tick, and neither do deaths. When the book asks for your hours, count the ticks.

The hours matter at the crossing to Gate 0. If you have ticked 4 hours or fewer, you will be rewarded there. If you have ticked 5, it will cost you 1 Claim. If you ever tick the sixth box, the gate has closed: turn straight to {E_FINALCALL}.

**Fighting.** Each round, roll two dice and add your Nerve, then do the same for your enemy. Whoever scores higher wounds the other for 2 Vigour. A tie wounds no one: fight another round. When your enemy's Vigour reaches 0, you have won, so read on. If yours reaches 0, you have lost.

**Chases.** Some things can't be fought, only outrun. When something comes after you, the book will tell you to test your Nerve, or, when only luck will save you, your Fortune. Succeed and you get away. Fail and it catches you, and the section says what that costs before you read on.

**Codewords and items.** When the book says "Note the codeword THAW" or "Note the HANDBOOK on your Adventure Sheet", write it down. When it tells you to cross one off, cross it off. They remember what you did, even when you'd rather forget.

Codewords are exact: THAW is not TRUCE. When a section asks whether you have one, only that word counts.

**Checkpoints.** Some section numbers are marked with ✈. Whenever you reach one, write its number in the LAST ✈ CHECKPOINT box on your Adventure Sheet. When a death sends you back, it names the section to return to: add to your Claim what it tells you, turn there, and choose again, with the rest of your Adventure Sheet as it was.

If your Vigour reaches 0, that is a death too. Add 1 to your Claim, turn back to the last ✈ section you visited, restore your Vigour to its starting score, and try again.

**Back to the beginning.** One ending sends you to section 1 to begin the night again. If it does, keep your Claim (but if it is more than 2, set it to 2) and keep your lore: everything you have read, you know. Reset everything else. Your Nerve, Vigour, Fortune and Fear return to their starting scores, and every codeword and item is crossed off. Keep SON, DAUGHTER or KID: that never changes.

**The Handbook.** When you find it, its rules are printed on the back of your Adventure Sheet. Believe them.
A01:
Gate 14. 11:52pm.

The seats are the hard plastic kind, bolted together in rows, so that when Sam shifts his weight two places down from you, you feel it in your spine. That's the closest you've been to your brother in three years.

Two seats apart. One empty one between you, which neither of you has put a bag on, which neither of you will.

He has had his earbuds in since the check-in queue, since the moment he saw you at the bag drop and said *hey* to a point somewhere over your left shoulder.

You are flying home to bury your father.

The departures board above the gate desk ticks over with that soft clatter you loved as a kid. *LV 137. Larkvale Airways. Boarding 00:20.* You check your phone, though there's nothing on it you haven't read. The funeral director's email. A text from your aunt: *Is Sam with you? Look after each other.*

You haven't answered that one.

The terminal is nearly empty. A cleaner pushing a floor polisher three gates away. A couple asleep on each other's shoulders. And at the far end of the concourse, past the last gate, a passenger in a long coat, much too tall, standing perfectly still and holding up a handwritten sign.

The kind drivers hold at arrivals, with a name on it. Whoever it's waiting for isn't here. This is departures.

It's too far away to read the name. You find yourself trying anyway, with the odd, tired feeling that you have tried before.

Then the board above you clatters, and every letter on it turns over.

Turn to {A02}.
A02:
*LV 137. DELAYED.*

No new time. Just the word, sitting there in amber where the boarding time used to be.

Sam takes out one earbud. Not both. One.

"Typical," he says.

It's the first thing he's said to you that isn't *hey* or *fine* or *I've got it*. You realise you've been bracing for it all day, the way you brace for the bump of a landing.

You could leave it there. You're good at leaving things there.

Or you could say something back. You haven't eaten since a cereal bar at the other airport, eleven hours and one time zone ago. Further down the concourse, one kiosk still has its shutter half up and a light on. *LAST ORDERS*, says a handwritten sign taped to the till.

Sam is looking at his phone, but he isn't scrolling.

If you ask Sam whether he wants to get something to eat, turn to {A03}.

If you stay where you are and phone your aunt instead, turn to {A04}.
A03:
"I'm getting food," you say. "Do you want anything?"

Sam looks at you for slightly too long. Then he pulls the other earbud out and stands up, which you didn't expect, and walks beside you to the kiosk without saying yes.

The cashier is a young man in a paper hat. You order two cheese toasties, a tea, and a hot chocolate, because Sam always had hot chocolate at airports, and your mouth remembered before you did.

Sam hears it. He doesn't say anything. He takes the cup.

The cashier counts your change onto the counter, coin by coin, and his gaze stays dry and fixed on your face. He doesn't blink.

The receipt curls out of the till. *14/03/1987  23:58.*

"Sam. Look at the date."

He laughs, a real one, short and surprised. "Nineteen eighty-seven. Classic Dad airport. He'd have loved that."

Then he hears himself say *Dad*, and the laugh stops.

Halfway back to your seats, you both look round. The shutter is down. The young man in the paper hat is standing behind the counter in the dark, watching you. He hasn't blinked.

In your pocket, the phone buzzes once.

*Missed call: Dad.*

*Voicemail: Dad. 05:59.*

The date beside the time is tomorrow's. Under it, one transcribed line, cut off mid-sentence: *"I should have told you both why I never…"*

You lock the screen.

"Who was that?" Sam says.

"Nothing," you say.

Turn to {A05}.
A04:
You call your aunt. It doesn't ring. The bars in the corner of your screen have been replaced by a single word: *SEARCHING*.

You try the airport Wi-Fi. It asks for your name. You close it.

There's a notification waiting, and you're sure it wasn't there a moment ago.

*Missed call: Dad.*

*Voicemail: Dad. 05:59.*

You check the date beside the time. It's tomorrow's.

The phone has done what phones do now and transcribed the start of it. One line sits on your lock screen like a note slid under a door, cut off mid-sentence:

*"I should have told you both why I never…"*

Your father has been dead for nine days. Gain 1 Fear.

Down the concourse, the kiosk's till chatters by itself and pushes out a receipt.

You don't play it. You lock the screen and put the phone face down on your knee, and when you look up, Sam is watching you.

"Who was that?" he says.

"Nothing," you say.

Turn to {A05}.
A05:
*Ding-dong.*

The chime is the old kind, two soft notes, the sound of every departure lounge you have ever sat in. The clock over the gate desk says 01:04. You don't remember the last hour going anywhere.

*Good evening. Larkvale Airways thanks all passengers for their patience.*

It's a kind voice. Unhurried. The kind of voice that tells you the cabin crew will be round shortly.

And every other person in the terminal stands up at once.

The couple who were asleep on each other's shoulders. The cleaner with the floor polisher. A man you hadn't noticed, lying flat across four seats with his coat over his face. They all stand at the same moment, pick up their bags, and walk towards the exit signs.

Not hurrying. Walking slightly faster than people walk. Nobody looks at anybody else.

You look at Sam.

Sam is asleep. Earbuds in, chin on his chest, arms folded the way Dad used to sleep in front of the television. You don't know when that happened. As far as you can tell, he was awake a minute ago.

The last of the crowd is turning the corner by the toilets. Whatever they know, they're taking it with them. If you're going to follow them, it has to be now.

If you get up and follow the crowd to the exit, turn to {A06}.

If you stay where you are, with Sam, turn to {A07}.
